activities.title: Core Concept: switch Statements
activities.content:
### switch Statements

Master the classic switch statement for multi-value exact matching on byte, short, char, int, String, and enums.

When testing a single variable against many fixed, discrete constants (such as menu options, HTTP status codes, or weekdays), chaining 10 else-if blocks becomes cluttered and repetitive. Java provides the `switch` statement: an efficient control-flow structure that jumps directly to the matching `case` label.

---

### 1. Anatomy of the Classic switch Statement

A switch statement evaluates an expression once, then compares the result sequentially against each `case` label:

```java
switch (expression) {
    case value1:
        // Code executed if expression == value1
        break;
    case value2:
        // Code executed if expression == value2
        break;
    default:
        // Fallback executed if no case matched
        break;
}
```

The `break` statement terminates the switch block immediately. Without `break`, execution continues right into the next case regardless of whether the condition matches — a behavior called **fallthrough**.

---

### 2. Supported Data Types in switch

Not all Java types can be evaluated inside a switch expression. Java permits:

1. **Primitive integer types**: `byte`, `short`, `char`, `int` (and their wrapper classes `Byte`, `Short`, `Character`, `Integer`).
2. **String**: Allowed since Java 7.
3. **Enum types**: Custom enumerated constants.

❌ **Types NOT allowed** in classic switch:
- `long`, `float`, `double`, `boolean`.
- Custom objects (unless enums).

---

### 3. The Fallthrough Mechanism: Danger and Intentional Use

If you omit `break`, Java does NOT stop executing. It cascades into the subsequent cases until a `break` or the end of the switch block is reached.

While usually an accidental bug, intentional fallthrough is useful when multiple cases share identical handling:

```java
int dayOfWeek = 6; // Saturday
switch (dayOfWeek) {
    case 1:
    case 2:
    case 3:
    case 4:
    case 5:
        System.out.println("Weekday");
        break;
    case 6:
    case 7:
        System.out.println("Weekend!");
        break;
    default:
        System.out.println("Invalid day");
}
```

---

### 4. Case Labels Must Be Compile-Time Constants

Every value following `case` must be a **constant expression** known at compile time. You cannot use normal non-final variables, method calls, or range operators:

```java
int target = 10;
final int MAX = 100; // Compile-time constant

switch (target) {
    case 10:   // OK: integer literal
    case MAX:  // OK: final compile-time constant
    // case > 5: // COMPILE ERROR: relational operators not allowed
    // case someVariable: // COMPILE ERROR: non-final variable
}
```

---

> [!NOTE]
> **Key Takeaway**:
> Use classic switch for discrete, constant value equality comparisons on int, char, String, or enum. Always terminate each case branch with `break` unless intentional fallthrough is explicitly desired.

questions.prompt: Which of the following data types CANNOT be used in a classic Java switch statement?
options: int
String
double
char
questions.explanation: Floating point types (float and double), boolean, and long cannot be used in a classic Java switch expression because floating point rounding makes exact equality matching problematic.

questions.prompt: What happens if a case branch in a classic switch statement omits the `break;` statement?
options: The program fails to compile with 'Missing break statement'
Execution cascades into the next case statement (fallthrough) regardless of whether the next case matches
The switch block loops infinitely
The JVM throws a RuntimeException at line of omission
questions.explanation: In Java, omitting break causes 'fallthrough': execution continues directly into the subsequent case statements until a break or the closing brace is encountered.

options: B
BC
BCD
ABCD
questions.explanation: x matches case 2, printing 'B'. Because case 2 has no break, execution falls through to case 3, printing 'C'. Case 3 has a break, terminating the switch. Result: 'BC'.

questions.prompt: Can two case labels have the exact same constant value in a switch statement?
options: Yes, both branches execute sequentially
Yes, but only if they are placed next to each other
No, the compiler flags a 'duplicate case label' error
No, only String cases allow duplicates
questions.explanation: Duplicate case labels are illegal in Java and cause a compile-time error. Every case label in a switch must be distinct.

questions.prompt: Which requirement must every case value in a classic switch statement satisfy?
options: It must be a compile-time constant expression
It must be an object reference initialized with new
It must be a boolean expression returning true
It must be enclosed in double quotes
questions.explanation: Case values must be compile-time constants (literals or final variables initialized with constant expressions). Variables whose values are resolved at runtime cannot be used.

questions.prompt: Where can the `default:` clause be placed inside a switch block?
options: Strictly at the very beginning before any case
Strictly at the very end after all cases
Anywhere inside the switch block (beginning, middle, or end)
It must follow case 0
questions.explanation: The default clause can be placed anywhere inside the switch block. However, placing it at the end is standard professional convention for readability. If placed earlier without break, it will fall through to subsequent cases.

options: Full Access
Access Restricted
Read-only
Compile error
questions.explanation: String matching in switch is strictly case-sensitive. "admin" does not equal "Admin". Therefore, the default branch executes, printing 'Access Restricted'.

questions.prompt: What happens if a switch evaluates a null String reference: `String s = null; switch (s) { ... }`?
options: It silently jumps to the default branch
It throws a NullPointerException at runtime
It fails to compile
It prints 'null'
questions.explanation: Under the hood, Java compiler compiles String switch into hashCode() and equals() calls. Passing null results in a NullPointerException before evaluating any case.

questions.prompt: When should an engineer choose switch over an if-else-if ladder?
options: When comparing complex ranges (e.g. score >= 80 && score <= 90)
When matching a single variable against multiple discrete constant values
When comparing floating-point numbers
When the variable is of type boolean
questions.explanation: Switch is ideal for multi-branch equality matching against discrete constant values. For range checks or boolean evaluations, if-else-if is required.

questions.prompt: How does the Java compiler optimize large integer switch statements under the hood?
options: By creating recursive function calls
By compiling into bytecode tableswitch (O(1) direct index jump) or lookupswitch (O(log n) binary search)
By converting it into nested while loops
By evaluating conditions on multiple CPU threads
questions.explanation: The JVM compiles dense integer switches into tableswitch (constant time O(1) jump table) and sparse ones into lookupswitch (binary search table O(log n)), outperforming linear O(n) chained else-if ladders.

practice.title: Day Planner Switch
practice.problemStatement:
Write a complete Java program in the Main class that declares an int variable `dayNumber` initialized to `3`. Using a classic switch statement, print the corresponding day name and routine:
- 1: "Monday: Team Planning"
- 2: "Tuesday: Deep Focus"
- 3: "Wednesday: Midweek Review"
- 4: "Thursday: Development"
- 5: "Friday: Code Release"
- 6, 7: "Weekend: Recharging"
- default: "Invalid Day Number"

Ensure every case uses break properly.
hints: For day 3, print 'Wednesday: Midweek Review' followed by break;
Remember to group case 6 and case 7 for weekend using fallthrough.

interviewQA.question: Why does Java disallow float and double in switch statements?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Floating-point numbers in Java adhere to IEEE 754 standards, where arithmetic operations can produce tiny rounding errors (e.g. 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004). Exact bitwise equality comparisons between floats are unreliable. To guarantee deterministic constant-time branching, Java restricts switch to types with exact, discrete values (integers, characters, strings, and enums).
keyPoints: Highlight IEEE 754 precision limitations and explain why exact equality is dangerous for floats in critical business systems.

interviewQA.question: What is the internal performance difference between switch and if-else ladders?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: An if-else-if ladder executes linearly in O(n) worst-case time by sequentially evaluating boolean expressions until one evaluates to true. In contrast, the Java compiler optimizes switch into either `tableswitch` (an O(1) direct index jump table when case values are dense) or `lookupswitch` (an O(log n) binary search table when case values are sparse). Therefore, switch statements outperform long if-else ladders as the number of branches increases.
keyPoints: Mention bytecode instructions `tableswitch` and `lookupswitch` — interviewers love candidates who understand bytecode-level optimizations.

interviewQA.question: How did Java 7 implement support for Strings in switch statements?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: The Java compiler de-sugars String switch into a two-step process: first, it switches on the String's `hashCode()` (an integer), jumping to candidates with matching hashes. Second, inside the matching bucket, it executes `.equals()` to protect against hash collisions. Because this calls `hashCode()`, switching on a null String immediately throws a `NullPointerException`.
keyPoints: Always note that passing null to a String switch throws NullPointerException before reaching the default branch.

interviewQA.question: What is intentional fallthrough, and when is it acceptable in clean code?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Intentional fallthrough occurs when multiple case labels share identical execution logic without repeating code (e.g. grouping cases 1 through 5 for weekdays and 6 through 7 for weekends). It is acceptable only when clearly structured and documented. Otherwise, accidental omission of break is one of the most common sources of production defects in classic Java.
keyPoints: State that Java 14+ switch expressions eliminate accidental fallthrough entirely using the arrow `->` operator.

interviewQA.question: Why can't non-final variables or expressions like `x > 10` be used in switch case labels?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Case labels must evaluate to compile-time constants so the compiler can precompute jump tables (`tableswitch`/`lookupswitch`) at compile time. Dynamic runtime expressions or relational conditions would require runtime evaluation, destroying the deterministic jump architecture of classic switch.
keyPoints: Emphasize compile-time resolution and constant expressions.

interviewQA.question: What happens if no case matches and there is no default clause?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: If no case matches and no default clause is present, the switch statement completes normally without executing any code block, and program execution continues with the statement immediately following the switch.
keyPoints: Professional code should always include a defensive default clause to handle unexpected inputs.

interviewQA.question: Can an enum be used in a switch statement? What is the syntax requirement?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Yes, enums are fully supported in switch statements. Crucially, when referencing enum constants in case labels, you must use the unqualified constant name (e.g. `case MONDAY:`) rather than the qualified name (`case Day.MONDAY:`), because the switch expression type already informs the compiler of the enum type.
keyPoints: Mentioning that qualifying enum names in case labels causes a compile error proves real hands-on Java experience.

interviewQA.question: Can variable declarations inside one case block conflict with declarations in another case block in classic switch?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Yes. The entire switch block constitutes a single local variable scope. If you declare `int temp = 10;` inside `case 1:` without enclosing that case in curly braces `{ ... }`, declaring `int temp = 20;` in `case 2:` results in a 'Variable already defined' compile-time error. Enclosing each case in its own `{}` block creates isolated lexical scopes.
keyPoints: Highlight the single-scope trap of classic switch and demonstrate how block braces `{}` fix it.

activities.title: Topic Confidence Checklist
checklist: Use classic switch for discrete equality comparisons on byte, short, char, int, String, or enum
Always terminate every case branch with `break;` unless intentional fallthrough is required
Place a defensive `default:` branch to capture unexpected or corrupted input values
Ensure all case labels are compile-time constants, not runtime variables
Check for null before switching on a String to prevent NullPointerException
